quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

subagents.description: Person evidence linking for Hermann Gaetjen

output.text_response:
No warnings on I1. All 14 links are written and the tree is clean.

---

The 1875 San Francisco Great Register names Hermann Gatjen, age 21, born in Germany, working as a fireman at 5 Cook Street, naturalized that same day — 13 August 1875 — in California's 4th District Court. A separate immigration index records a Herm Gaetjen, born 1854 in Prussia, arriving in New York on 2 June 1871. These two records almost certainly describe the same man: the birth year 1854 appears in both, the unusual surname is identical (with one being a slight spelling variation), and the route — landing in New York at 17, then settling in San Francisco by age 21 — is a coherent life trajectory. That person fits Hermann Gaetjen (I1) on name, sex, location (in San Francisco three years before his first child was born there in 1878), and German origin. The only friction is that the tree currently shows I1 born "about 1859," but that date has no source attached to it; both records independently say 1854, so the tree estimate is very likely simply wrong.

However, there are two other men named Hermann or Herman Gaetjen documented in California — one born in 1873 (too young to have been a voter in 1875), one born in 1827 and dead in Butte County by 1899 (too old, wrong county) — and because those namesakes are on record, the system requires a formal "tie" before it will accept even a probable link to I1. That tie would come from another person in the same record who can be independently connected to I1's family (such as a spouse or child), or from a previous record showing I1 at the same address or occupation. Neither of these records contains any other named party, so both are entered as **"only possible" links to I1**, not "probable" ones. No facts from either record have been copied onto I1's profile as a result.

To move these links from "only possible" to "probably Hermann Gaetjen I1," the next step is to find a record that either names Amelia Nichols together with this same Hermann Gaetjen, or shows Hermann Gaetjen at a consistent address or occupation in a source that is itself already tied to I1 — a marriage record, an 1880 census entry, or a city directory entry would all accomplish this.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

agent_returns.text:
No warnings on I1. All 14 links are written and the tree is clean.

---

The 1875 San Francisco Great Register names Hermann Gatjen, age 21, born in Germany, working as a fireman at 5 Cook Street, naturalized that same day — 13 August 1875 — in California's 4th District Court. A separate immigration index records a Herm Gaetjen, born 1854 in Prussia, arriving in New York on 2 June 1871. These two records almost certainly describe the same man: the birth year 1854 appears in both, the unusual surname is identical (with one being a slight spelling variation), and the route — landing in New York at 17, then settling in San Francisco by age 21 — is a coherent life trajectory. That person fits Hermann Gaetjen (I1) on name, sex, location (in San Francisco three years before his first child was born there in 1878), and German origin. The only friction is that the tree currently shows I1 born "about 1859," but that date has no source attached to it; both records independently say 1854, so the tree estimate is very likely simply wrong.

However, there are two other men named Hermann or Herman Gaetjen documented in California — one born in 1873 (too young to have been a voter in 1875), one born in 1827 and dead in Butte County by 1899 (too old, wrong county) — and because those namesakes are on record, the system requires a formal "tie" before it will accept even a probable link to I1. That tie would come from another person in the same record who can be independently connected to I1's family (such as a spouse or child), or from a previous record showing I1 at the same address or occupation. Neither of these records contains any other named party, so both are entered as "only possible" links to I1, not "probable" ones. No facts from either record have been copied onto I1's profile as a result.

To move these links from "only possible" to "probably Hermann Gaetjen I1," the next step is to find a record that either names Amelia Nichols together with this same Hermann Gaetjen, or shows Hermann Gaetjen at a consistent address or occupation in a source that is itself already tied to I1 — a marriage record, an 1880 census entry, or a city directory entry would all accomplish this.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Here is the person-evidence agent's report:

---

**No warnings** on I1. Person warnings check is clean.

**Materialization status:** Because all `pe_` links are marked `speculative`, the tool requires at least a `probable` link before writing facts onto tree person I1. Materialization was not attempted. The facts from both records — name, occupation, San Francisco residence, naturalization date from the 1875 Great Register; 1854 birth year, Prussian origin, 1871 New York arrival from the immigration index — cannot be incorporated into I1's tree record until the birth year discrepancy is adjudicated and confidence can be raised.

---

**Summary of Findings**

Two historical documents were matched to Hermann Gaetjen in the family tree:
1. **1875 San Francisco Great Register** — Hermann Gatjen, age 21, born Germany, fireman, 5 Cook Street, naturalized 13 Aug 1875, California 4th District Court.
2. **Germans to America Index** — Herm Gaetjen, born 1854 Prussia, arrived New York 2 Jun 1871.

Both records tell a consistent story: a young German man, born around 1854 in Prussia, arrived in New York in 1871, made his way to San Francisco, obtained citizenship on 13 August 1875, registered to vote that same day, and three years later his first child was born in San Francisco.

**The two other California Hermann Gaetjens are ruled out:** one was not born until 1873; the other was born in 1827 and would have been 48 (not 21) in 1875. That makes the family tree's Hermann Gaetjen the only plausible match.

**Why only "speculative" for now:** The tree currently shows Hermann's birth year as *about 1859*, but both records independently indicate *about 1854* — a five-year gap. Notably, California law in 1875 required a voter to be at least 21 years old; if Hermann had truly been born in 1859, he would have been only ~16 at naturalization — legally impossible. The 1859 date in the tree is unsourced, so it is almost certainly a rough estimate.

**Recommended next step:** A brief conflict-resolution check to formally update the birth year from the unsourced ~1859 to ~1854, which would allow the links to be promoted from `speculative` to `probable` and would permit the full historical facts (1871 arrival, Prussian origin) to be written directly onto Hermann's tree record.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly identified and linked the three assertions from the 1860 census record. However, pe_004 (a_010 → I1) was already linked before this run, and the skill created pe_009 (a_010 → I2) as the 'other-side' link to Thomas Flynn. Per the per-test context, linking a_010 to its second party (the head Thomas/I2) is acceptable and not a duplicate. The skill correctly avoided re-linking a_010 to Patrick. However, the confidence levels assigned to pe_007 and pe_008 are problematic: both are marked 'confident' despite being single-source links with no independent corroboration on the 1860 record itself. The rubric states that 'confident' requires multiple independent sources corroborating the identity link, and a single census record is 'probable' at best. The rationale claims 'I1 is independently corroborated by prior records (1850 census and death record)' but those are separate records, not independent corroboration within this linking decision—the 1860 record alone does not warrant 'confident.' This is a one-tier overstatement of confidence.
